Applied AI PM: the route, week by week (19 Oct 2026 – 18 Apr 2027)

On this tab
  1. How a week works
  2. Month 1: The problem and the plan
  3. Month 2: Meet the machine
  4. Month 3: Finding, and your first system
  5. Month 4: What real systems add
  6. Month 5: The same ideas, at production depth
  7. Month 6: Ship it, and get the job
  8. Staying on the route

This plan is the course. It has one row for each week, and each row lists the steps of the route in order: a book chapter to read, then the playbook chapter that practises it, sometimes a small try, and a look back on Friday. The same steps, in the same order, are on the route page in the playbook and at the end of each chapter in the book.

Progress is shared too. Mark a chapter complete in the playbook, or read a book chapter to its end, and the tick shows up here. Tick a try or a look back here, and it shows up in the playbook. Sign in once and the ticks follow you to every device. The reasons behind the route are on the Curriculum tab, and how to take each kind of step is on the How to build tab.

Loading your progress…

Restart the calendar

Fallen behind the dates? Start week 1 again on any day you choose. Your ticks and notes stay as they are; only the dates move, so the week you are on becomes this week. The playbook and the book follow the same dates.

North star: by 18 April 2027, Bharat Privacy Guard is shipped and evaluated, with a findings document and a demo you can take into an interview.

How a week works

A week is a handful of steps. Most take ten to twenty minutes, so most days need one step. On a day when even that feels like too much, do one page and tick it.

StepWhat you doWhen it ticks
BookRead the chapter in the book, in English or HinglishBy itself, when you reach the end
ChapterRead it in the playbook, answer the boxes, do the hands-on stepsWhen you press “Mark chapter complete”
First passFor Track A and Track B: read and answer the boxes; the long Build waitsWhen you press “Mark chapter complete”
TryA small task off the pageWhen you tick it, here or on the route page
Look backThree lines in your notepad on FridayWhen you tick it

How to read the weekly rows

  • Time: the total for the week’s steps. Month 1 is about an hour a week, and it builds slowly to about four or five hours in each of the two capstone weeks.
  • By Sunday: the thing the week leaves you with. Put a link or a note in the row if you want a record.
  • How to: links to the How to build tab.
  • Going further: optional outside reading for a week with spare energy. It is never required.
  • Holiday weeks (W10 and W11): about half an hour each, by design.

Month 2: Meet the machine

W516 Nov – 22 Nov~70 min

Meet the machine

Why nowYour plan needs a model, so now you meet one. The book explains what it is. Chapter 0.5 shows tokens and cost on your own text, before anything is set up.

Staying on the route

Everyone drifts at some point. So the plan decides in advance what you will do when it happens: carry on from the first open step, smaller if you need to. Never skip steps to catch up, and never go down to zero.

The rules

  1. One route. The playbook, the book and this plan follow the same steps in the same order. If two of them ever disagree, the route page in the playbook wins, and that is a bug to report.
  2. Story first, then the chapter. Read a chapter’s story in the book before you do the chapter in the playbook.
  3. Ten minutes is a real day. On a bad day do one page and tick it. A small day counts; a zero day does not.
  4. Never miss twice. One missed day is life. Two in a row is a new habit.
  5. Behind is fine. Carry on from the first open step; the dates are a guide, not a judge. Never skip a step to catch up.
  6. First pass now, the long build later. The “Build it” sections in Track A and Track B are optional on the route. Write “later” next to them and move on.
  7. Parking lot, not action. New courses, tools and side projects go in the parking lot and wait for the monthly review.
  8. Friday look back. Three lines in your notepad every week: what made sense, what didn’t, one question.

Parking lot

New ideas, courses and side projects come here first. You look at them again only at the monthly review.

Friday look back (5 minutes)

Write three lines in your notepad:

  • What made sense this week.
  • What didn’t, yet.
  • One question you still have.

Then tick the week’s look-back step. If you keep a photo log, take the photo now.

Tripwires: if this happens, do this

A tripwire is a warning sign you decide on in advance. Here is what to do for each one.

If this happensDo this
You missed a dayNothing special. Do the next open step tomorrow
You missed two days in a rowDo one page today, however small, so it never becomes three
You are two weeks behind the datesKeep going from the first open step. The dates are a guide. Move the end of the plan rather than skipping steps
You feel the urge to start a new course, app or toolWrite it in the parking lot, close the tab, and open the route
A work crunch is comingDecide on Sunday that the week will be ten minutes a day, before the crunch starts
You haven’t opened anything for 7 daysOpen the route page today and do the step marked next. One page counts

Monthly reviews

At the end of each month, spend 20 minutes on the review. Check the month against its line below, tick it, and look through the parking lot.

M115 Nov 2026

The first four weeks ticked, or nearly: the book’s first seven chapters read, and A1 to A7 done on a first pass right after each one.

If behind: If you missed days, do not catch up in one go. Carry on from the first open step and let the dates slide.

M220 Dec 2026

A model connected, your first model call costed, a system prompt tested, your first answer key, and a sorter with a score.

If behind: Never cut the first model call. If time is short, keep the answer key and do the summary chapter on a first pass.

M317 Jan 2027

Search by words and by meaning compared on a scoreboard, version 0 of the findings page published with a link, and an extractor that says “not sure”.

If behind: Publish the findings page with whatever numbers you have. An honest short page beats a perfect missing one.

M421 Feb 2027

The attack on your own tool, a checked automatic marker, a cost model, the system card, the requirements and the build-or-buy call.

If behind: Do the chapters on a first pass and keep one hands-on result per week.

M528 Mar 2027

Your model choice with a back-up, the tool access policy, the release gate, the risk register and the decision pack.

If behind: If time is short, keep the release gate and the risk register; the others can be one page each.

M618 Apr 2027

Bharat Privacy Guard shipped with its findings document and demo, a portfolio page, and three practice interviews.

If behind: Do not cut this one. Move it into May rather than skip it.

If you are a month or more behind: stop and decide on purpose. Either carry on and move the end date, or make the next month lighter (first pass only). Quietly abandoning the route is the only option that’s ruled out.

How to do the work, and how to ship it

The Plan & tracker tab lists every step of the route. The steps themselves live in the playbook and the book, which explain each idea and the hands-on work in full. This tab covers what sits around them: how to take a chapter on its first pass, the one-time setup, and how to publish what you make so other people can see it.

What "shipped" means

An item is shipped when a stranger could open one link and see it. Anything less is still a draft. Use this checklist when a week asks you to publish:

  1. A public link. This can be a GitHub repo, a GitHub Pages page, a Hugging Face Space or a published post. A file on your machine doesn’t count, and neither does a private repo.
  2. A page that opens with the result. Put the number first, for example "the sorter got 47 of 50 right". Then explain how it works.
  3. One honest failure. Show a case where it still breaks. This is what separates an evaluated product from a demo.
  4. Public data only. Use the made-up records the course gives you. Never use client data, and nothing covered by an employer or client NDA.
  5. A ship-log line. One line in your log every Sunday: the date, the week, what you finished (recipe).

If you run out of time, publish at 80%. A decent page that is public beats a perfect one that nobody can see.

A chapter on its first pass

Weeks 1–24. Ships: the week’s steps ticked. Time: what the route says for each step.

Every week on the route is a few steps in order: a book chapter, then the playbook chapter that practises it, sometimes a small try, and a look back on Friday. Read the story first and do its chapter the same day or the next, while the story is fresh. Here is how to take each kind.

  1. A book chapter. Read it in the book, in English or Hinglish. It ticks itself when you reach the end, on every page of the site and in your account. A chapter split over two days ticks its first half when you reach the second.
  2. A playbook chapter. Read it and answer the boxes as you go. Do the hands-on steps that run in the browser. Then press “Mark chapter complete” at the end; that is what ticks the step.
  3. A first pass. Track A and Track B have long “Build it” sections. On the route you read the chapter, answer its boxes and mark it complete. Write “later” next to the Build in your notepad and come back to it when you have time.
  4. A try. A small task off the page. Do it, then tick it on the route page or on this tab.
  5. The look back. Three lines in your notepad: what made sense, what didn’t, and one question. If you keep a photo log, take the photo now. Tick it.

Done when: every step of the week shows a tick. If a week runs over, carry on from the first open step next week. The dates are a guide, not a judge.

The one-time setup

Week 5. Ships: a model connected and the test call working. Time: about 15 minutes, once.

The setup lives in one place: the setup page in the playbook. You get a free API key, paste it in once, and press the test button. The code in every chapter then runs right there in the page, with nothing installed and no other window. It comes right after Chapter 0.5, where you saw tokens and cost on your own text, so you know what the key pays for.

  1. Do one section at a time. Stop after any section if the day’s ten minutes are up.
  2. If a step fails, the page says why. Copy the exact error message into your notes, with the step you were on.
  3. The key stays in the setup page, in your browser. Never paste it into a code cell or a chat.

Done when: the setup page’s test cell prints setup works.

Publish a project

Weeks 12 and 25. Ships: a public write-up with a link anyone can open. Time: 2 hours, strictly time-boxed.

Publishing is what turns finished work into something other people can see. In Week 12 you publish version 0 of the findings page; in Week 25, the capstone. Keep to the two hours, and stop when the time is up.

  1. Put the write-up in the repo README (or docs/report.md), in this order: Result (one headline number), Problem, What I built (one diagram or screenshot), How I evaluated it (data, metrics, method), What failed (two examples and the counts), Cost and latency, What I would do next, Reproduce.
  2. Tag a release (v1.0), so the version you describe stays frozen.
  3. If the project has a visual or a demo, publish it for free. Use a static page on GitHub Pages, or an app on Hugging Face Spaces.
  4. Record a short demo (demo-video), and link it at the top of the README.
  5. Post on LinkedIn in three sentences: the result with its number, one thing that surprised you, and the link. Write it in English, with a Hinglish example if it helps.
  6. Add the Sunday ship-log line (ship-log).

Done when: you can send one link to a stranger and they can understand the result in 60 seconds.

Demo video: three minutes, no editing

Week 25. Use any screen recorder (Loom, or your phone recording the screen). Only the screen is needed, not your face. Keep the video to three minutes. Here is a simple script to follow:

  1. 0:00–0:20: the problem, in one sentence, and the result number.
  2. 0:20–2:00: a live run on two inputs, one that works and one that fails or is refused.
  3. 2:00–2:40: the eval table, or the CI gate turning red and green.
  4. 2:40–3:00: what you would do next. Do one take, and leave small stumbles in.

Upload it as unlisted, and link it at the top of the README.

Portfolio site

Week 26. Ships: a live page for Bharat Privacy Guard. Time: 3–4 hours.

This is the front door to your work. Keep it plain, quick to read, and honest about numbers.

  1. Create a repo named <your-username>.github.io, or any repo with Pages enabled (quickstart). Plain HTML or Markdown is enough.
  2. Give the project one page, in this order: problem, approach, evals, result number, failure example, what you would do next, and links to the findings document and demo video.
  3. Add a short home page: who you are in two sentences, the project as a card with its headline number, and how to reach you. Add later projects as cards when they exist.
  4. Check it on a phone, and fix anything that overflows. Then ask one person to find your best result in under 30 seconds.

Done when: the link works in a private browser window and the project card shows a number.

Mock interviews

Week 26. Ships: three practice interviews with written answers, then eight stories from your own career. Time: about 90 minutes for the three, and more after the route if you are interviewing.

You’ll practise out loud, because answering in your head is much easier than answering in words. Start with product-sense and evaluation questions, then stories from your own career.

  1. Use the question bank and Exponent's product sense guide. Pick questions you would find hard. Ask Claude or Gemini to interview you with a rubric (problem framing, why AI, metrics, evals, failure handling, cost) and to score you. Then repeat your worst answer.
  2. Answer out loud, and record yourself. Write your final answer to each question in your own words. The written answers are the deliverable.
  3. Use this structure: user and problem, why AI or not, approach, behavior in failure, metrics (product, model, guardrail), evals, cost and latency, risks, launch plan.
  4. Then write 8 STAR stories from your own career (Situation, Task, Action, Result with a number). Cover a killed feature, a disagreement with a senior stakeholder, shipping under ambiguity, a failure and recovery, and a time you used data to change a decision.
  5. Prepare a direct answer to "why AI PM, given your project-management background?" Start it with what you shipped and evaluated on this route.
  6. Do one mock take-home: a 3-hour product exercise, written up in 2 pages.

Done when: three practice answers are written down. The stories and the take-home can follow after the route.

Retro: review the six months

Week 26. Ships: a one-page review and the next learning loop. Time: about 3 hours.

This is the last week. Look back at what you did, take what worked forward, and decide what comes next.

  1. Read your ship log. Count what shipped, what slipped and what you cut.
  2. Update the portfolio site with any metric that changed.
  3. Write down what worked, and what you would change for the next six months.
  4. Set the after-the-route loop at 3 hours a week: 60 minutes of reading release notes, a monthly session re-running your capstone test set on a new model and writing down the difference, and the second pass on one Track A or Track B “Build it” each month.

Done when: the review is written and the next three Sundays are decided.

Ship log: one line every Sunday

Keep the log wherever you write every day: your notepad, a private note, or a SHIPLOG.md file. It looks like this:

2026-10-25  W1  Start here, the preface and book chapters 1-2. First three lines.
2026-11-15  W4  Ten test messages: the chat assistant got 8/10. Missed the phone number written in words.

A ten-minute week still gets a line. A missing line means a zero week.

Applied AI PM Curriculum (Oct 2026 – Apr 2027)

  2. Six-month route at a glance

This is a 26-week route to becoming a believable Applied AI Product Manager by April 2027. It runs from Monday 19 October 2026 to Sunday 18 April 2027. It starts at about an hour a week and builds slowly from there. Everything runs in the browser, and no local machine is needed.

There is one route, and three places show it. The playbook is where you do each chapter. The book tells the same chapters as one story, in the same order. This plan shows the route as weeks, with notes and monthly reviews. All three read the same list and the same progress, so a chapter you mark complete in the playbook, or a book chapter you finish, is ticked everywhere.

There are three tabs here. The Plan & tracker tab is the route week by week. The How to build tab explains how to take a chapter on its first pass, the one-time setup, and how to publish. This tab, the Curriculum, explains the reasoning, and keeps the job-market research and interview preparation.

Bottom line

You can be a believable Applied AI PM candidate by April 2027, on one condition. You need to come across as someone who owns technical products and delivery, and who has built and tested working AI. Someone who has only read about AI won’t get the same hearing.

So the route ends with one shipped, evaluated product: Bharat Privacy Guard, the course’s project. You build it a piece at a time, chapter by chapter, and publish it with its numbers in Week 25.

The route in one paragraph: the route follows the book’s order, and every week pairs a book chapter (the story) with the playbook chapter that practises it, so the two are never weeks apart. Month 1 is the product half: the problem, its users, its market, a plan and a spec, with no code. Month 2 meets the machine: tokens, a model connected, just enough Python to read the code, the first call, instructions, an answer key, sorting and summarising. Months 3 and 4 build and measure the core: search, the first complete system, dependable output, attacks, grading at scale, cost, the rules and the spec. Month 5 goes over the same ideas at production depth. Month 6 ships the capstone, covers the business and gets you ready for interviews.

Weekly time

The route starts small on purpose. Month 1 is about an hour a week. Months 2 to 4 are one and a half to two hours. Month 5 is about three. The two capstone weeks ask for about four or five hours each. If you have more time, carry on to the next step. The route never stops you going ahead, and the dates are a guide, not a judge.

Job-market grounding

Before we plan anything, let's look at what employers want. Demand is strong. But the bar has moved. Employers now expect you to be fluent in evals and to have shipped real things.

Demand signals

Three signals are worth knowing. Each comes with a caution, because job numbers are easy to misread.

  • Global: Lenny's early-2026 job-market report (TrueUp data) counted 7,300+ open PM roles at tech companies. That is the most since 2022. It also said AI roles are "absolutely exploding."
  • India: foundit's 2025 tracker counted about 2.9 lakh AI-linked postings. It projects roughly 32% growth in 2026, and that is a projection, not a result. Aggregator counts include duplicates and loosely related roles. So read them as a direction, not as a size.
  • Pay (India): Glassdoor India shows an average of about ₹29 lakh a year. But it comes from only 27 reports, so treat it as a rough guide. US benchmarks from KORE1 are $165K–$238K base. Remote roles at US pay bands for India-based PMs exist, but they are rare.

What real 2026 job descriptions ask for

Now let's read some real postings. The table has one posting per row. The middle column shows what the posting asks for. The last column shows what that means for you.

Answer it with shipped agents, eval reports and Product Owner language

One gap is worth noting. Government AI units, such as Digital India Corporation (home of BHASHINI), hire for AI roles under titles like Business Analyst (AI) or Principal Architect. They don't use "AI Product Manager." We also couldn't verify any AI PM postings at PwC or Accenture India.

What distinguishes strong candidates

Across all those postings, five things keep coming up. Here they are, in the order I'd work on them.

  1. Eval ownership. KORE1's guide lists two signs of technical fluency: owning the design of eval sets, and sitting in model design reviews. Exponent notes that OpenAI leaders call writing evals a core PM skill.
  2. Artifacts over claims. You need one shipped product (a side project is fine), one written case study with real numbers, and one eval suite that someone can run. This comes from an Institute of PM guide. That site is a training vendor, but its advice matches every posting above.
  3. Knowing when not to use a model. KORE1's interview rubric grades this instinct as seriously as the design itself.
  4. Failure-mode design. Decide how much hallucination each product can tolerate. Measure it all the time, and design fallbacks.
  5. Owning cost per task and latency. Field guides now describe this as part of the AI PM's job.

Interview formats in 2026

Interview loops are changing too. Here is what we know, company by company.

  • Structure: Northeastern's 2026 guide names four shifts. There is a dedicated AI product-sense round. Every loop has technical drill-downs. Behavioral questions probe deeper. And estimation questions have almost disappeared.
  • Meta added a "Product Sense with AI" round. Candidates vibe-code a working prototype (Exponent).
  • Anthropic: the final loop has about five panels in one day. The product-sense cases include safety tradeoffs (IGotAnOffer).
  • OpenAI: 4–6 rounds over 1–2 days. Some candidates get a take-home case to present (Exponent).
  • Consulting and Indian firms: a recruiter call, a hiring manager, a case or PRD exercise, then a panel. Take-homes are common at startups.

Skills rising toward 2027, in order of evidence strength

Here is a list of the skills that are growing fastest. The ones at the top have the most evidence behind them.

  1. Evals and error analysis for agents (trajectory evals, validated LLM-as-judge)
  2. Agent design with MCP/A2A interoperability, human-in-the-loop and autonomy levels
  3. Context engineering
  4. Cost and latency economics as first-class product metrics
  5. AI governance operations (EU AI Act transparency, DPDP consent, India's sector-led approach)
  6. Voice and multimodal products, especially Indic voice-first
  7. Live prototyping with coding agents in interviews

Books (buy at most two)

  • **Chip Huyen, AI Engineering** (O'Reilly, 2025). This is the best single reference if you want technical depth as a PM. Read the chapters on evaluation, RAG and agents, inference optimization and the feedback loop.
  • **Hamel Husain and Shreya Shankar, Evals for AI Engineers** (O'Reilly, listed for late October 2026, about 225 pages). It was not out yet on 7 Oct 2026. So pre-order it, or read it on O'Reilly when it arrives.

The route, month by month

Each table lists the weeks of one month. The weeks themselves, with every step, are on the Plan & tracker tab.

Month 1: The problem and the plan (W1–4, 19 Oct – 15 Nov 2026)

You read the book from its first page: the story of a product manager in Pune who finds identity numbers in a week of customer chats, and decides whether that deserves a year of work. Each book chapter is followed in the same week by its playbook chapter, A1 to A7, on a first pass: you read the method and answer its boxes while the story is fresh. There is no code and nothing to install. By the end you have a problem, its users, its market, a plan and a short spec, all for the project you will build.

The project: Bharat Privacy Guard

The course builds one project from start to finish. Bharat Privacy Guard is a small tool that sits between a person and a website, an app or an AI chatbot. It spots Indian identity numbers and other personal details in what someone is about to send, and warns them or covers the details before they leave. The project page in the playbook shows its thirteen stages and which chapters build each one.

It is a good portfolio project for a GovTech product manager for three reasons. It touches the DPDP Act directly. It needs evaluation at every step, from a small answer key in Month 2 to a release gate in Month 5. And it can be built entirely on made-up records, so nothing private is ever used.

Definition of done (Week 25): a public findings document that opens with its headline numbers, an honest failure example, the cost per check, a three-minute screen-recorded demo, and a link anyone can open.

Interview preparation

Use one shape for your AI product-sense answers. Go through these in order: the user and problem; why AI (or why not); the model approach; behavior in failure and trust moments; metrics (product, model, guardrail); evals; cost and latency; risks; and the launch plan. Drill with the question bank and your own projects, and follow the mock-interview recipe.

Here are 19 practice questions, in five groups.

AI product sense

  1. Design a voice-first grievance-filing assistant for rural citizens who speak Bhojpuri. How do you handle low-confidence speech recognition?
  2. Should DigiLocker add an AI assistant? What do you build first, and what do you refuse to build?
  3. Design an AI feature that saves users time without eroding trust.
  4. How would you measure the success of a new frontier model release?

Evals and metrics

  1. Write the evals for a travel-booking agent. What is the difference between final-answer and trajectory evals?
  2. Your LLM judge says 92% pass but users complain. What do you do?
  3. A model version bump drops your eval scores 4 points on Hindi queries only. Walk me through your response.
  4. What evals would you run before shipping a new model to enterprise customers?

Technical depth

  1. When would you choose RAG vs fine-tuning vs a longer context window?
  2. Explain prompt caching and how it changes unit economics.
  3. What is MCP, and what security risks does it add? How do you mitigate prompt injection through tool outputs?
  4. Your agent costs ₹6 per task and the business case needs ₹1. List five levers.

Strategy, governance and economics

  1. Build vs buy for an Indic-language assistant for a ministry: frontier API, Sarvam open-weight or BHASHINI?
  2. What does the 13 May 2027 DPDP deadline change in your roadmap for an AI feature that processes citizen data?
  3. An EU customer asks whether your HR screening feature is "high-risk." What do you answer, and what changed with the Digital Omnibus?

Behavioral (match each one to a real story from your own career)

  1. Tell me about a time you killed or descoped a feature.
  2. Tell me about a time you disagreed with a senior government stakeholder, and how you resolved it.
  3. Tell me about a time you shipped under ambiguity, with incomplete requirements.
  4. Why AI PM, and why now? Prepare a direct answer to the "transitioning from project management" objection, and start it with the AI work you have shipped.

Future-proofing for 2027

By 2027, agents, evals and governance operations will be standard PM responsibilities. So the habit of re-running your own evals will matter more than any single course.

Likely changes (forecasts, based on current evidence)

These are forecasts, not facts. Treat them as the direction of travel.

  • Agents become the default unit of product. MCP now sits under neutral governance at the Linux Foundation's Agentic AI Foundation, and A2A covers agent-to-agent work. PMs will specify autonomy levels, approval flows and agent evals.
  • Evals become a standing function, not a project. Expect eval CI, production trace review and judge validation to appear in more job descriptions.
  • Regulatory milestones in and just after your window: DPDP Consent Managers (13 Nov 2026), EU Article 50(2) watermarking (2 Dec 2026), full DPDP compliance (13 May 2027), and EU high-risk Annex III obligations (2 Dec 2027). India's proposed AI governance institutions may be set up, but neither is final.
  • Sovereign and Indic AI deepens. The IndiaAI Mission is funding 12 organisations that are building indigenous models. BHASHINI now runs on sovereign cloud. Expect more government RFPs that ask for Indic, on-prem or open-weight options. That plays to your GovTech background.
  • Free API tiers keep shrinking. Budget for a little paid usage, and keep your projects model-agnostic.
  • Interviews will include live building. Keep a weekly 45-minute prototyping habit.

After the route (about 3 hours a week)

After April you don’t stop. You keep a light loop going, at four speeds.

  1. Weekly (60 min): Read Lenny's Newsletter, Hamel's blog, the MCP changelog, DeepLearning.AI's The Batch, and the release notes from Anthropic, OpenAI and Google.
  2. Monthly (90 min): Re-run your capstone test set on the newest models and write down what changed. Do the second pass on one Track A or Track B “Build it”. A benchmark you keep alive builds your credibility over time.
  3. Quarterly: Write one new teardown, and one post on regulation updates in India and the EU.
  4. Annually: Decide on AIGP if you are moving towards governance-heavy roles. Refresh your portfolio.

Caveats and uncertain claims

Some of the research above is weaker than the rest. Treat these items with care.

  • Job-count numbers: The Lenny/TrueUp counts cover tech-company roles. The India aggregator counts (Glassdoor, foundit, LinkedIn) include duplicates and adjacent roles. And foundit's 2026 figure is a projection.
  • Salary data: India AI PM salary data is thin (27 Glassdoor reports), and some aggregator estimates are clearly wrong.
  • Job postings: Several come from aggregators (Instahyre, Weekday, DreamWorkHQ) and may be closed or mislabeled. The PhonePe listing's description looks mismatched. Check postings on the employers' own career pages.
  • Course details: Claude Academy course counts vary by source because the catalog grew during 2026. Maven prices and dates change with each cohort. Marily Nika's "#1" and alumni figures are self-reported.
  • Unpublished book: Evals for AI Engineers was listed for late October 2026, and was not out yet on 7 Oct 2026.
  • Regulatory dates: The EU AI Act dates follow Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, as law-firm sources report it. India's AI Governance Guidelines are voluntary. The proposed institutions had not been set up in the reports I found.
  • Free tiers: Gemini free-tier limits vary by source and change without notice. Check the live limits in AI Studio.
  • Interview loops: Reports on Meta, OpenAI and Anthropic interviews come from prep companies and candidate accounts, not from the employers' own documents.
  • Cost estimates: All the INR budget figures are my planning estimates, not quoted prices.
